headline: RBA not finished hiking; base case is a long, slow global tightening cycle with at least one more rise from 4.6%, mirroring the drawn-out mining-boom tightening cycle
reasoning: Ivan Colhoun argues the RBA's 25bp hike to 4.6% was well-telegraphed but the press conference signalled continued gradualism rather than urgency. He believes 4.6% is insufficient to bring inflation down by 1%, particularly given the AI investment boom and high energy prices. His base case is a prolonged global rate tightening cycle — drawing the analogy to the six-year mining-boom tightening cycle — with at least one more hike, possibly several. He does not think a recession is inevitable but warns interest-sensitive, highly indebted and discretionary-spending sectors will feel recessionary conditions.
quote: I think I personally think, uh, we're in this, as we know, massive investment boom. If you look back in history, when you have investment booms, Interest rates tend to rise a lot for a lot longer and a lot higher than people expect, but they tend to do it slowly. So in the mining boom in Australia, we had I think it was a six year tightening cycle. So my base case has been we're in a long slow global rate tightening cycle. And I think the central banks, the gradualism I heard yesterday um I think that's going to persist. Uh, and so I think there'll definitely be another rate rise. Um, but there may be a few more.
episode_title: Businesses face higher rates and the rising risk of insolvency

headline: Unemployment to drift higher gradually rather than spike; last month's number was distorted by unusual ABS seasonal adjustment; watching Seek job ads as a key leading indicator after August improvement
reasoning: Ivan Colhoun believes the unemployment rate will drift higher rather than jump sharply, and dismisses last month's print as a 'furphy' attributing it to unusual ABS seasonal adjustment and survey changes, suggesting the real rate remains around 4.5%. He notes that Seek job ads actually improved in August, and is watching closely whether that trend continues in coming months, which would change his view materially. A rapid rate-hiking scenario would heighten unemployment risk, but current indicators point to only a slow rise.
quote: I think it will drift higher. I think last month's number was a furphy. Uh, I think that ABS did some unusual seasonal adjustment and changes to the survey. So I think unemployment's still at 4.5%. Um, job ads, very interestingly. Seek job ads went up last month, so I'm watching that space. Uh, if they picked up in in the next couple of months, uh, then it would be telling me a very different story. Uh, but, uh, it's I think it will drift up rather than, uh, jump up sharply. Now, if they were tightening interest rates much more quickly, then that's when you get the risk. But the indicators I follow are saying, uh, at best a slow rise at worst, sorry, a slow rise in the unemployment rate.
episode_title: Businesses face higher rates and the rising risk of insolvency

headline: Discretionary, high-debt and interest-sensitive sectors will feel recessionary pain; technology, mining and data-centre construction will remain resilient
reasoning: Colhoun sees the Australian economy as highly bifurcated: sectors with heavy debt loads, discretionary spending exposure or interest sensitivity will experience conditions that feel like recession, while technology, parts of mining, and construction and services tied to data-centre build-out will continue to perform well. He does not call an economy-wide recession as his base case but sees a very uneven outcome depending on sector.
quote: Do we have to have a recession? No, but I think parts of the economy will find it quite challenging with higher interest rates, with higher energy prices. So if you've got a lot of debt, if you, um, are interest sensitive, um, if you're discretionary spending, it will probably feel like a recession in those sectors. But technology, parts of mining, other parts of construction, building data centres and services to those areas are going to find that times are pretty good. So it's quite a diverse economy, uh, that these set of circumstances is leading to.
episode_title: Businesses face higher rates and the rising risk of insolvency

headline: Payment defaults have picked up sharply in the last 3–4 months, signalling a further wave of business insolvencies ahead
reasoning: CreditorWatch data shows insolvencies have been plateauing at an elevated level, but a key leading indicator — payment defaults (when a company formally registers that another company is not paying its invoices) — has risen significantly in the past three to four months. Colhoun interprets this as a forward signal that insolvency volumes will increase in the period ahead, consistent with the broader macro backdrop of higher rates and energy costs.
quote: One of our key indicators that we track is, um, payment defaults. And that's when a company isn't or a company registers that another company is not paying its invoices. Now, that measure has picked up quite a bit in the last 3 or 4 months. So that's giving us a signal. I think, that we need to expect more insolvencies in the period ahead. I think the general macro conditions we're facing tell us that same story.
episode_title: Businesses face higher rates and the rising risk of insolvency

headline: Wages growth running at 3.5–4% is an underappreciated base-level cost driver keeping domestic inflation elevated
reasoning: Colhoun argues that wages growth, now running at 3.5–4% versus around 2.5% when inflation was near 2%, is a persistent and underplayed driver of domestic inflationary pressures. Combined with Covid-era cost increases, the energy shock, higher construction costs and rising rents, businesses face a very broad-based cost increase. He thinks this wages dynamic, rather than government spending, is the more important structural story for inflation.
quote: I look at it and I think of wages. Firstly, um, if you went back to when inflation was around 2% and, you know, people were, I think, foolishly worrying about inflation being too low, um, wages growth was much lower. It was running somewhere around 2.5%. Now we've seen wages growth for the last few years, um, running in that three and a half, 4% rate. Uh, and so that's a base level of, uh, cost growth. Uh, we've seen a lot of other costs rise, um, through Covid rates. Um, and then we've got the energy shock, uh, that we've currently experiencing.

headline: Interest-sensitive consumer discretionary sector under increasing pressure from higher petrol prices and rising rates; insolvencies have based and expected to head higher
reasoning: Colhoun describes an increasingly divergent economic picture across Australian sectors. Consumer discretionary, being interest-sensitive, will feel the combined squeeze of higher petrol prices and further rate hikes. He notes that insolvencies appear to have bottomed and are likely to rise from here, with consumer-facing businesses among those most exposed.
quote: I think what you're seeing is a increasingly divergent economic picture by sector. So the interest sensitive parts of the economy, residential real estate and consumer discretionary will will feel the pressure from those higher petrol prices, higher interest rates. But the AI investment boom, the related strength in in mining prices, I think that's helping those sectors perform. And even within residential real estate and construction or non residential construction, you'll see two different sectors there. So really a more diverse economic picture, we're not seeing that so much in insolvencies just yet, but they are, they look like they've based and the expectation is they'll probably head up a bit from here.

headline: RBA has made a clear-cut case to tighten in September; July CPI and higher oil prices have already materialised the upside inflation risks flagged in the last minutes
reasoning: Colhoun interprets the RBA's recent communications as a clear signal that staff will recommend a cash rate increase to the Monetary Policy Board. He notes the board minutes from the last meeting explicitly warned about upside inflation risks, which he now views as having already materialised via higher oil prices and the July CPI print. While nine board members vote and only two are from the RBA itself, he regards a September tightening as the most likely outcome.
quote: The way I interpret that is the staff and the RBA, when they write the board paper, we'll recommend the cash rate is increased to the Monetary Policy Board. Of course, there's nine members on that board and only two are from the RBA, so it doesn't guarantee that a rate rise will happen. But the minutes from the last meeting really was saying that the board will have more information by this meeting. They talked about really worrying if some of the upside risks of inflation came through or became more likely. I think they're actually already reality with that higher oil prices, the July CPI. So I think it's a pretty clear case that a clear cut case they'll tighten in September.
episode_title: Ivan says Fed hikes are back on the table

headline: Fed very likely to hike this week, with two more hikes expected before mid-next year; rates unlikely to come down anytime soon given the inflationary nature of the AI investment boom
reasoning: Ivan Colhoun notes the market has rapidly repriced a Fed rate hike to 90% probability, up from just over 50% a week ago. He argues central banks and markets have been slow to recognise that the investment phase of the AI boom is inherently inflationary. He expects the Fed to raise rates this week, again likely in December, and once more in the first half of next year. He cautions that investment booms historically involve long, slow tightening cycles, so rate cuts are unlikely anytime soon.
quote: I think the market has finally caught on to the fact and fully priced that a rate hike is very, very likely. I think it's 90% price now. Week ago that was just over 50%. So I think central banks in the market have been quite slow to pick up on the fact that the investment phase of the AI boom actually is inflationary. So I think that's been important in the moves of the last week, as has that much higher oil price as well. So central banks are just getting frustrated in trying to return inflation to target. So what I'm expecting is the Fed to raise rates this week, probably raise rates again before Christmas, most likely December, and then another rate hike, you know, first half of next year. And then I think 3 moves will probably do it in the short term. But this is an investment boom. Investment booms usually have very long and slow tightening cycles. So unfortunately, I don't see a likelihood that interest rates are coming down anytime soon.
episode_title: Ivan says Fed hikes are back on the table

headline: Higher oil prices are an external supply shock the RBA cannot directly fix, but tightening is still warranted to prevent inflationary expectations and wage pressures becoming entrenched, and to slow the economy enough to return inflation to target
reasoning: Colhoun acknowledges that raising interest rates cannot address the source of oil-price inflation but argues the RBA's concern is preventing second-round effects: higher oil prices feeding into wage demands and construction cost pressures amplified by the AI-driven investment boom. The bank needs the economy to run a bit slower to ensure these external shocks do not become embedded in expectations, justifying tightening even against a supply-side shock.
quote: No, look, it's a good point. It you can't, no matter what the Reserve Bank does with interest rates, it won't open the Strait of hummus. But what the bank will be, the way I think they'll be thinking about it is they need to make sure that these higher oil prices don't get into expectations, don't lead to higher wage rises. We're seeing the AI boom likely to pressure the construction cycle. If prices are higher, materials prices go up, then the chances of wage demands rising going up, I think rises as well. So it's more that with these external developments, the Reserve Bank needs the economy to run a bit slower if it's going to get inflation to return to that target.

headline: Higher bond yields driven by a cocktail of oil-price inflation, AI funding demand, government deficit borrowing, and repriced Fed rate-rise expectations; Trump's $5,000 midterm promise adding further fiscal stimulus risk
reasoning: Colhoun identifies multiple concurrent drivers pushing global bond yields higher: oil prices lifting near-term inflation, massive funding demand from both AI investment and widening government budget deficits, and markets repricing the probability of Fed rate hikes.
